summary.text: The Lorentz transformations convert the space and time coordinates of an event from one frame to another frame moving at constant velocity relative to it.
They replace the Galilean transformation of Newtonian physics, which is a good approximation only at speeds much less than the speed of light.
They let observers disagree about distances, elapsed times and even the order of events, while every one of them measures the same speed of light.

facts.label: Speed limit
facts.value: Relative speed v must be smaller than c

facts.label: What stays fixed
facts.value: The spacetime interval between any two events

facts.value: Adding translations gives the Poincare group

items.prompt: A rocket is firing its engines hard and speeding up. Can the Lorentz transformations link its frame to Earth's frame?

options.label: Yes, they work for any frame at all
No, they refer to transformations between frames with no acceleration
Yes, but only once its engines have stopped firing
No, because rockets are too small to count

items.explain: The term refers only to transformations between inertial frames, which move at constant velocity.

items.prompt: Two observers in relative motion disagree about the order in which two events happened. Does this break the theory?

options.label: Yes, since events must have one fixed order
Yes, unless their clocks were synchronized
No, but they must at least agree on the distances
No, the transformations allow it while keeping light speed the same

items.explain: Observers at different velocities may measure different distances, times and orderings, always so that light speed is the same in all inertial frames.

items.prompt: A car and a rocket both use the Lorentz transformations, but the car's answer looks just like the old Galilean one. Why?

options.label: The car's speed is tiny next to light, so the Lorentz factor is nearly 1
Cars are made of ordinary matter rather than particles
Lorentz's formulas only apply to light itself
The car's frame has no clocks to compare

items.explain: When speed is much smaller than c, the Lorentz factor is negligibly different from 1, and the Galilean version is a good approximation.

items.prompt: A student plugs a relative speed bigger than the speed of light into the transformation and gets nonsense. What is the lesson?

options.label: The formula needs more decimal places to work
It only works below the speed of light
The student must switch to Galilean formulas instead
The nonsense shows the frames are accelerating

items.explain: The value of v must be smaller than c for the transformation to produce functional solutions.

items.prompt: Two observers in different inertial frames each calculate something about the same pair of events. Which quantity do they agree on?

options.label: The time between the events
The spacetime interval between them
The distance between the events
The order in which they happened

items.explain: In Minkowski space the Lorentz transformations preserve the spacetime interval between any two events.

items.prompt: Before 1905 the transformations were used with an aether to explain light's speed. What did Einstein do differently?

options.label: He derived them from two principles and dropped the aether as unneeded
He kept the aether but added a moving frame to it
He measured them directly in the lab for the first time
He borrowed Voigt's version without changing it

items.explain: Einstein derived the transformation from the principle of relativity and constant light speed, abandoning the aether as unnecessary.

paragraphs.heading: Switching viewpoints
paragraphs.text: The Lorentz transformations are the rules for converting coordinates from one frame in spacetime to another frame moving at a constant velocity relative to the first. They act on events, where an event is something that happens at one point in space at one instant, a single point in spacetime. The transformations link the space and time coordinates that observers in each frame give to the same event. They form a linear family with six parameters, named after the Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz.

paragraphs.heading: Replacing Galileo
paragraphs.text: They take the place of the Galilean transformation of Newton's physics, which assumes an absolute space and time. Galileo's version is a good approximation only when relative speeds are much lower than the speed of light. The Lorentz version has some unintuitive features: observers moving at different velocities can measure different distances, different elapsed times and even a different order of events. Through all of that, the speed of light stays the same in every inertial frame, which is one of the postulates of special relativity.

paragraphs.heading: Only steady motion
paragraphs.text: Frames of reference come in two kinds: inertial ones, in relative motion at constant velocity, and non-inertial ones, which accelerate, follow curved paths or rotate. The name Lorentz transformation is used only for changes between inertial frames, usually in special relativity. In each frame an observer measures lengths with a local coordinate system, usually Cartesian, and time intervals with a clock.

paragraphs.heading: A geometric view
paragraphs.text: A Lorentz transformation can include a rotation of space; one with no rotation is called a Lorentz boost. In Minkowski space, the model of spacetime used in special relativity, these transformations keep the spacetime interval between any two events unchanged. They leave the event at the origin fixed and can be pictured as a hyperbolic rotation of Minkowski space. Adding translations as well gives a larger set known as the Poincaré group.

paragraphs.heading: From aether to Einstein
paragraphs.text: In the 1890s Lorentz was building theories of electrodynamics around an aether, and from 1892 to 1904 he used these transformations as mathematical aids. Woldemar Voigt had developed similar ones in 1887 while studying the Doppler shift. That same year a more accurate repeat of the Michelson–Morley experiment led George FitzGerald to suggest that bodies moving through the aether contract, an idea Lorentz presented independently and in more detail in 1892. In 1905 Henri Poincaré recognized that the transformations form a mathematical group and named it after Lorentz. That same year Albert Einstein derived them from the principle of relativity and the constant speed of light, setting the aether aside as unnecessary.
